name: Dropax (Roman pitch plaster)

lead: Dropax is the name given in antiquity to a pitch-based depilatory plaster. It was spread on the skin and pulled away, taking hair with it, giving a smooth, hairless surface of the kind valued in Greco-Roman grooming.

It belongs to the long history of hair removal. Descriptions come from classical writers rather than modern trials, so how well it performed and how it felt are known mainly through historical accounts.

paras: Historically, a sticky resin or pitch plaster was applied to the area and then peeled off in one movement, a principle that survives in modern waxing. Hair removal in Rome was often carried out by specialist attendants at the baths.

Sticky pitch removed from skin can cause pain, irritation and skin lifting, and hot resin can burn. No modern studies of dropax exist, and modern waxing products are formulated and regulated differently.

chain: Plaster pulled off with the hair
angle.text: Dropax removed body hair by adhesion, leaving the skin smooth for as long as the hair took to regrow. It is the ancestor of today's waxing methods.

lead: Dropax was a depilatory used in ancient Greece and Rome, described as a pitch plaster that removed unwanted body hair when pulled from the skin.[1] Together with the paste-like psilothron, it is one of the named hair-removal products of the classical world.[1]

Smooth skin was part of grooming for many in the Roman world; slaves called alipili removed body hair for bathers, and female attendants called paratiltriae served women.[1] The adhesive-plaster approach of dropax is conceptually close to modern waxing and sugaring, which also lift hair from the root.
No clinical research exists on dropax itself; what is known comes from historical summaries of classical practice.

paras: Classical-era hair removal used several products. Dropax and psilothron are both recorded as depilatories in Greece and Rome.[1] Dropax is associated with pitch applied as a plaster rather than a paste that is wiped off.

Hair removal itself was often delegated: bathers could be attended by alipili, and women by paratiltriae.[1] Suetonius wrote that the emperor Augustus used hot nutshells on his legs, showing that varied methods were in circulation.[1]

sections.h: In the history of hair removal
paras: Depilation was common in ancient Egypt among the wealthy, using pumice and razors, and abrasive pastes of lime, ash and orpiment were also used in antiquity.[1] Later milestones include the first safety razor in 1760 and early 20th-century marketing of hair removal to women.[1] Dropax sits among these early, pre-industrial techniques.

Pulling hair from the skin with an adhesive can cause pain, redness and irritation, and heated pitch raises burn risk. Specific records of injuries from dropax are not covered here; the statement reflects general features of adhesive depilation.

timeline.event: Dropax and psilothron recorded as depilatories in Greece and Rome.[1]
First safety razor invented in Paris.[1]
